extracted.intended_audience: IP office statisticians, trademark researchers, policymakers, and IP practitioners analysing global trademark data
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological standards for measuring, comparing and interpreting trademark application and registration activity across offices and origins (use of class counts, resident vs non‑resident breakdowns, adjustments for GDP/population, Nice classification and sector groupings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application class count (harmonization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total number of classes specified in applications – known as the application class count – is used to harmonize differences between filing systems and to improve international comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many offices allow single‑class or multi‑class filing; comparing application counts across offices is made more meaningful by using class counts. This method for comparing offices began in 2004 (first year of complete class count data). Use application class counts to make trademark registration and filing internationally comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nice Classification usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications are classified according to the Nice Classification; applications can refer to one or more of the 45 Nice classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nice classes group goods and services (e.g., goods class 9: scientific, photographic, measuring instruments, recording equipment, computers and software; services class 35: advertising, business management; services class 42: scientific and technological services). Use the Nice classes as the basis for class‑count statistics and mapping to sectors (see www.wipo.int/classifications/nice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office data vs origin data perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark application statistics can be analysed from two distinct perspectives: office data (applications received by a particular office, capturing resident and non‑resident applicants) and origin data (applications organised by the applicant's country/place of residence, encompassing resident filing and abroad filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both perspectives are complementary: office data describes activity at a specific office; origin data describes where applicants reside and their filing behaviour domestically and abroad. Use the appropriate perspective depending on the analytic question (e.g., office workload vs applicant internationalization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by origin: absolute count vs equivalent count
rubrics_metrics.description: Origin data can be calculated based on either absolute count (an application filed at a regional office is counted once) or equivalent count (an application filed at a regional office is counted multiple times). Data reported in this section are based on absolute count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which counting convention is used when comparing origin statistics across sources; absolute count avoids double‑counting regional filings whereas equivalent counts reflect multiplicity at regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs non‑resident filing distinction and shares
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident filing refers to applications filed at an applicant’s home or regional office; non‑resident (abroad) filing comprises filings made at foreign offices. In 2024 resident filing constituted 84.1% of global total and non‑resident 15.9%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret changes in resident/non‑resident shares cautiously — shifts can reflect large domestic filing growth in a single economy (e.g., China) or changes in applicant internationalization. Examine contribution of resident vs non‑resident filing to total growth at each office to identify drivers of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of class counts to compare offices and registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Class counts are used to compare application and registration activity across offices and over time, enabling more meaningful international comparisons than raw application counts alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing registrations to applications, note that registrations in a given year may reflect applications from prior years and are influenced by an office’s examination resources and processing capacity. Therefore, do not directly equate applications received in a year with registrations issued in the same year without accounting for processing lags and resource changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment for GDP and population for cross‑country comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident trademark application class counts should be adjusted for economic size (GDP) and population to account for cross‑country differences in scale and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples used: resident application class count per USD 100 billion GDP and resident application class count per million population. These adjusted measures highlight filing intensity relative to economic output and population (e.g., China, Türkiye, Brazil rank high on GDP‑adjusted metrics; Republic of Korea high on per‑million population metric). Use these adjustments to compare filing intensity rather than absolute volumes alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping Nice classes into industry sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate the 45 Nice classes into a smaller set of industry sectors (the report groups them into 10 industry sectors) to analyse sectoral filing patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sectoral grouping permits insights such as which industries attract the most intensive non‑resident filing (e.g., research and technology, health, clothing and accessories). Use consistent class‑to‑sector mappings when comparing across offices and origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of top Nice classes and sectors for non‑resident filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the distribution of non‑resident filing by Nice class and sector: in 2024 goods class 9 and services classes 35 and 42 were among the top classes; the research and technology sector accounted for the largest share (19.3%) of non‑resident filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class‑level and sector‑level shares to detect industry patterns in international filing behaviour. Report the top classes/sectors and their percentage shares to characterise filing composition across destinations and origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration metrics and active registrations (stock measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrations are a distinct metric from applications; registrations can be maintained indefinitely through renewals. Active trademark registrations in force are a stock measure (e.g., an estimated 93.2 million active registrations in 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because registrations reflect completed examinations and renewal behaviour, their year‑to‑year counts are affected by office processing capacity and renewals. Compare registration class counts and retention rates (percentage of registrations remaining in force by registration year) to assess longevity and the stock of marks, but avoid equating registration counts with contemporaneous application volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑resident filing concentration and effects of regional systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some offices receive a large share of applications from non‑residents (e.g., EUIPO, Australia, Canada, UK, US), while others receive mostly domestic filings; regional offices like the EUIPO alter national non‑resident shares (many applicants use EUIPO instead of individual EU national offices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting non‑resident shares at national offices, account for regional filing routes that shift filing away from national offices (e.g., the EUIPO effect leads to lower non‑resident percentages at some EU member state offices). Analyse non‑resident flows between specific origins and offices to explain concentration patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of filing‑abroad choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants select foreign jurisdictions for trademark protection based on market attractiveness, geographical proximity and historical ties between home and destination countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flow data (origin→office matrices) and top source shares at key offices to interpret strategic motives for abroad filing (e.g., China‑based applicants dominate non‑resident filing in the US and EUIPO; US applicants lead foreign filing in several Americas and Asian offices). Consider these strategic factors when explaining cross‑border filing patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data completeness and annotation conventions (caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some data elements are incomplete or not applicable: 'Applications by origin data are incomplete, because some offices do not report by origin.' The report uses '..' to indicate not available and 'n.a.' to indicate not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag incomplete origin reporting and missing values when using aggregated totals or conducting cross‑country comparisons. Explicitly document any offices excluded from origin‑based analyses and apply caution when interpreting trends that might be driven by incomplete reporting.
